description: A tag is a representation of a value that someone has picked, like recipients for an email or categories on a planner task.
whenToUse: Tags create a visual pattern that lets people know they can change or remove the selection. To show system-generated data that people can’t change, use a badge instead.
states: Tag: Use a tag when you only need to provide information and when the only possible action is dismissal.
Interaction tag: Use an interaction tag when you can provide more information or actions related to what the tag represents.
behavior: Dismissal: Both tag types are optionally dismissible. Enable dismissal actions to let people undo their choices.

Non-dismissible tags communicate that a selection is not editable in the current context. Use them to continue the visual pattern that people can change the selection when they enter an editable state.

Interaction tag primary and secondary actions: In addition to dismissibility, interaction tags can have one other action. Don’t include actions that may be irrelevant or disruptive to the task at hand.
The secondary action in an interaction tag is always dismiss.
Reflow and overflow: By default, tags will reflow onto the next line if they can’t fit the container.
Optionally, you can include an overflow tag by using a tag of the same size and changing the primary text to +n, where n is the number of tags not displayed.
Tags that represent overflow must be interaction tags, so that people can interact to get more information.
Tags with wrapping behavior

Tags with overflow behavior: Consider a person’s goals when applying reflow and overflow behavior. For example, if it’s helpful for someone to see a list of tags to edit or remove them, make sure they wrap so all tags are visible.
Minimally, there should be 4 pixels of space between extra small tags, 6 pixels between small tags, and 8 pixels between medium tags.
Read the layout and spacing guidelines to learn how to appropriately apply space around tags.
Medium
Small
Extra small
accessibility: Tag interaction states: By default, tags have no interaction states and are static elements. If optional dismissibility is enabled, hover and focus states will also be enabled on the entire tag container.
Because interaction tags always have available actions, their interaction states are always enabled.
Truncation: Don’t truncate tag content. It’s important for people to understand at a glance what the tag represents so they can know how to interact with it.

do: Consider a person’s goals when applying reflow and overflow behavior.
Use the tag for the main info
dont: Don’t truncate tag content. It’s important for people to understand at a glance what the tag represents so they can know how to interact with it.

name: Tag picker
description: A Tag picker combines a text input and a dropdown giving people a way to select an option from a list or enter their own choice. These selections are represented as tags.
behavior: Selecting from a dropdown: When a user clicks into a tag picker, they invoke a dropdown that shows a list of items the user can choose. These are provided by the system and can represent files, people, and meetings.

Type to filter and select: Users can type when focused on an input to filter the list to match exactly what they’re looking for. Active descendant will always land on the first item, and will be the closest match to what the user has typed.
Secondary action: A tag picker provides a secondary action slot for extra functionality if needed. An example would be the option to “Clear all” tags within the input.

Wrapping tags: By default, tags that get inserted to the input wrap and will make the height grow to fit the content. Text within tags themselves can truncate, although it’s not provided out of the box as it is heavily opinionated by the product.
Truncating text in tags: If truncating is needed to fit in more content, a max width can be assigned so that if text in a tag exceeds it, it will truncate.
accessibility: Provide a clear name for the input: Use aria-label on TagPickerInput to provide an accessible name for the input. This attribute helps screen readers understand the purpose of the input.
Deletion interaction: When TagPickerInput is focused, pressing Backspace will remove the last tag. This behavior should be communicated to the user to avoid confusion.

do: Use aria-label on TagPickerInput to provide an accessible name for the input.

name: Text
description: The text component codifies Fluent's opinions on typography to make them easy to use and standardize across products.
whenToUse: Use the text component for plain text. For hypertext, try a link instead.
states: For easy implementation, use the text preset components. The presets map to the main text styles defined in the Fluent 2 Web UI kit.
Presets don’t allow for altering font family, size, or weight. If you need to adjust any of these attributes, use Text with the appropriate props.
behavior: Font families: Use the font prop to choose a font family. Stick with the base font, Segoe UI, in most scenarios.
Alignment: The align prop allows you to change text alignment. In most cases, left aligned text is the easiest to read.
Avoid justified text in web pages. The consistent line length and inconsistent spacing might make scanning information more difficult.
For more info, see our typography guidelines.
accessibility: By default, text components result in span elements. Use the as prop to produce semantic HTML.
Avoid using the appearance of a font to convey meaning. Bold and italic text should be used only when necessary, as not all screen readers communicate when text is bold or italicized.

do: Use the font prop to choose a font family.
dont: Avoid justified text in web pages. The consistent line length and inconsistent spacing might make scanning information more difficult.
Avoid using the appearance of a font to convey meaning. Bold and italic text should be used only when necessary, as not all screen readers communicate when text is bold or italicized.

name: Textarea
description: A textarea allows people to enter long, free-form text data, like a comment.
whenToUse: If you only need someone to enter one line of information, try an input instead.
behavior: By default, textareas are not resizable. If there is overflow content, the textarea will scroll.
The size of the textarea should fit the approximate volume of the content you expect people to enter.
accessibility: Don’t use placeholder text in the textarea for essential information that people will need to complete the textarea. If you do include placeholder text, be sure it is combined with a label.
Placeholder text must be associated with an aria-label for assistive technologies.
Include a label and use the placeholder to reinforce it
Don’t put too much information in the placeholder

do: Include a label and use the placeholder to reinforce it
dont: Don’t use placeholder text in the textarea for essential information that people will need to complete the textarea. If you do include placeholder text, be sure it is combined with a label.
Don’t put too much information in the placeholder

Don’t use placeholder text for essential information, which should appear either in the label or in helper text below the textarea, so it’s always visible. If you do include placeholder text, be sure it is combined with a label.

name: Toast
description: A toast communicates the status of an action someone is trying to take or that something happened elsewhere in the app. Toasts are temporary surfaces. Use them for information that's useful and relevant, but not critical.
whenToUse: For critical messages, try a modal Dialog, Field error, or Message bar instead.
states: Toasts generally fall into three categories: confirmation, progress, and communication. The toast component has slots that can be turned on and off to best help people achieve their goals.
Confirmation toast: Confirmation toasts are shown to someone as a direct result of their action. A confirmation toast’s state can be success, error, warning, informational, or progress.
Progress toast: Progress toasts inform someone about the status of an operation they initiated.
Communication toast: Communication toasts inform someone of messages from the system or another person’s actions. These messages can include mentions, event reminders, replies, and system updates.
They include a call to action directly linking to a solution or the content that they reference. They can be either temporary or persistent.
behavior: Dismissal: Toasts can have timed, conditional, or express dismissals, dependent on their use case.
Timed dismissal: If there is no action to take, toast will time out after seven seconds. Timed dismissal is best when there is no further action to take, like for a successful confirmation toast.
People who navigate via mouse can pause the timer by hovering over the toast. However, toasts that don’t include actions won’t receive keyboard focus for people who navigate primarily by keyboard.
Conditional dismissal: Use conditional dismissal for toasts that should persist until a condition is met, like a progress toast that dismisses once a task is complete.
Don’t use toasts for necessary actions. If you need the encourage people to take an action before moving forward, try a more forceful surface like a message bar or a dialog.
Express dismissal: Include the Close button to allow people to expressly dismiss toasts only if they can find that information again elsewhere, like in a notification center.
Determinate and indeterminate progress: Progress toasts can be either determinate or indeterminate, depending on the needs of your app and the capabilities of the technology you’re building on.

When the completion time can be predicted, show a determinate progress bar and percentage of completion. Determinate progress bars offer a reliable user experience since they communicate status and assure people things are still working.
If the completion time is unknown or its accuracy is unreliable, show an indeterminate spinner icon instead. Don’t show both a spinner and a progress bar in the same toast.
Don’t use both a spinner and a progress bar in a toast
Keep location predictable: Toasts should always appear in a consistent location within your app, where they are least likely to block the main content. This is usually the top-right or bottom-right.

Choose a location that works best for your product. For example, if you can toggle a notifications drawer from the top-right, place toasts there as well so that people will become used to looking for information in that part of the layout.
Place toasts in a consistent location
Don’t block the main content
Don’t overload the toaster: Toasts are wrapped in a container that handles their positioning, called a toaster.

New toasts always appear at the edge of a layout, pushing older toasts in the toaster toward the center. For example, if the toaster is at the top of the screen, a new toast will appear at the top and push any older toasts down.
Don’t show more than four toasts in a toaster and keep 16 pixels of space between them.
Stack up to 4 toasts
accessibility: Use the intent prop to properly determine the semantic styles, icons and aria-live regions and roles used in the toast.

All feedback states except info have an “assertive” aria-live and interrupt any other announcement a screen reader is making. Too many interruptions can disrupt someone’s flow, so don’t overload people with too many assertive toasts.

do: Use conditional dismissal for toasts that should persist until a condition is met, like a progress toast that dismisses once a task is complete.
Include the Close button to allow people to expressly dismiss toasts only if they can find that information again elsewhere, like in a notification center.
Place toasts in a consistent location
Use the intent prop to properly determine the semantic styles, icons and aria-live regions and roles used in the toast.
Give people the most accurate description of progress possible.
Write button labels that are specific responses to the main message in the title.
dont: Don’t use toasts for necessary actions. If you need the encourage people to take an action before moving forward, try a more forceful surface like a message bar or a dialog.
Don’t use both a spinner and a progress bar in a toast
Don’t block the main content
Don’t show more than four toasts in a toaster and keep 16 pixels of space between them.

name: Toolbar
description: A toolbar gives access to frequently used actions related to someone’s current view or task, like text formatting in an editor.
behavior: Overflow: A toolbar will grow to fit its parent container but will never wrap onto a second line. In cases where there are more options than can fit, use the overflow utility.
Create logical groupings: Actions in a toolbar should be logically grouped to help people find related subtasks. Use dividers and white space to communicate groupings.
If there are destructive actions or actions that can affect the status of someone’s work, group them away from other options.

Toolbars support the main task: Place toolbars so that they’re useful when people need them, with the commands that people are most likely to want. For example, in a text editing app where someone’s focus is always on creating content, it makes sense to have the toolbar with formatting options pinned to the top of the app.
When a toolbar isn’t supporting the main task, add an option for it to be hidden so that people can focus without distractions.
accessibility: Identify multiple toolbars: If an app contains more than one toolbar, each one should be labeled using aria-label or aria-labelledby if there’s an available text label.

Icons as button labels: Toolbars can use icons as button labels as a space-saving measure when there are many options to present. It’s important to use icons that are familiar and not force people to guess what each icon does.

do: Keep text labels on toolbar buttons or in tooltips brief.

name: Tooltip
description: A tooltip provides supplemental, contextual information elevated near its target component.
whenToUse: Tooltips should be used to provide helpful but non-essential, plaintext information. Don't use them to communicate system feedback. If you need to deliver robust, formatted information, use a popover instead.
behavior: Tooltips are triggered on hover or focus of the target component and dismissed on blur or mouse-out of the target or tooltip container.

By default, tooltips are placed 4 pixels away from their target element on hover or focus. Adjust the tooltip’s placement using system spacing tokens to ensure the tooltip doesn’t obscure important information.
In busy layouts, consider using an info button to indicate there’s more information within a tooltip.
accessibility: For screen reader users, connect tooltips to their target element with an id attribute and aria-describedby.

name: Tree
description: A tree is used to display a hierarchical view of nested data. It's useful for representing a menu structure, folder hierarchy, or nested categories at a glance. Each tree has a parent node and one or more levels of child nodes that can expand or collapse.
whenToUse: To show or hide information without regard to hierarchy, use an accordion instead. For information that's organized in a simpler structure, consider using a list or table instead.
states: Basic tree: A basic tree item displays text and icons, and can have interactive buttons appear on hover.
Persona tree: A persona tree item displays an avatar or image alongside text and sometimes includes additional metadata.
Item types: Each item in the tree represents a data point. Depending on its position in the tree, it’s classified either as a branch (parent) or a leaf (child) in the tree.

Branches are always parents, sometimes children: Use branches to group related items into categories and subcategories within a hierarchical tree structure. A branch is always a parent of some items, but might also be a child of another item.
A leaf is a child only: A leaf is a child item that contains no other child items below it. Leaf items signify the end of the branching path.
behavior: Interaction modes

Expand-and-collapse only: Expand-and-collapse-only mode is useful to show how information is organized. People can select any branch to expand it to show child nodes, and can select the branch again to hide them.
Navigation: In navigation mode, people can still expand and collapse items by selecting the chevron. But they can also select an item to see a detailed view on another surface.
Multiselect: Multiselect mode can be useful for performing batch operations on multiple items, such as deleting or moving them, or for selecting multiple items to view or edit at once.
Selecting a parent item also selects all of its children
If a child item is deselected, the parent checkbox shows a mixed selection state.
Reflow and overflow: By default, the content of each tree item wraps. The maximum width is defined by the container that it sits in.
However, you can change the behavior of tree items from wrapping text to truncating. Only choose this if truncated items are still easily differentiated from one another at a glance.
A tree item has several optional additions, including icons, badges, and quick actions.
Icons: Use simple, easily recognizable icons. Avoid complex or abstract icons that might confuse users.
Leading icons
Trailing icons

Badges: Badges can be used to provide more information about a node or to indicate its status. For example, a badge could indicate unread messages, recently updated, needs attention, or the number of child nodes that the node contains.
Each badge provides a text equivalent in a tooltip on hover.
This tree item has badges to indicate that something needs attention (!) and one new notification (1).

Quick actions: Quick actions can be added to tree items to provide contextual information and functionality without cluttering the UI or requiring the user to click on the node. For example, a quick action can trigger a pop-up menu that allows the user to perform actions on the node, such as editing its properties or deleting it.

When a tree node has both badging and quick actions, the default behavior is for the quick actions to replace the badges. However, if it’s necessary to keep the badges visible while hovering, they can be pushed to the side to make room for the quick actions.
For accessibility, make sure that these actions are also available by a more visible method, such as a toolbar or menu. Limit the number of quick actions to one or two at the most.
accessibility: Customization options such as the positioning of icons before or after a tree item are communicated to screen reader users through their slot properties.
To help screen readers understand the purpose of the tree overall, use the aria-label to provide an accessible name for the tree.

Quick actions are accessible for navigation, but are an unexpected pattern according to WAI-ARIA. To mitigate this, make sure that all quick actions are also available by an alternate method, such as a toolbar or menu.

do: Use sentence style capitalization—only capitalize the first word.

name: Chat input
description: The chat input is the area in a Copilot chat where a user can enter their Copilot prompt or question. It’s aimed more at conversational UX than durable content generation. If you need a component to help people create entities, try the Prompt input.
behavior: The submit button is hidden until the user inserts content into the textarea.
The add button opens a menu with options to add files, people, meetings, and other entities to the prompt, or to chat with an agent.
Suggestions appear above the chat input, and the AI generated disclaimer is shown below it.

Chat input is a highly composed Copilot pattern and, on its own, doesn’t dictate many UX behaviors. Instead, to understand how to help users get the most of this pattern, see the documentation for its component parts.

name: Attachment
description: An attachment represents an entity that Copilot should use for grounding a response. They appear as interactive tags in the input footer.
behavior: Loading: Use the loading state of the attachment to communicate that it’s being included in the Copilot prompt.
Handoff: Selecting the attachment title will initiate handoff and open the file in the appropriate app.
Dismissal: Attachments are always dismissible so people can choose to remove and change attachments as needed. Attachments can be dismissed by selecting the dismiss button.

Attachment list overflow: When attachments reach the max width of 180 pixels, remaining attachments collapse into an overflow menu. The overflow menu can also display a loading state to indicate that there are more attachments that are processing than the ones currently in view.
Attachments in the overflow are dismissible from the menu.
Naming attachments: Attachments should match file names exactly. Exclude the document type from the attachment name.
Attachment icons: Use the icon slot to indicate what type of file the attachment is. Keep logical relationships between visual indicators in the icon slot and attachment types.

do: Use the loading state of the attachment to communicate that it’s being included in the Copilot prompt.

name: Suggestions
description: A suggestion is a helpful prompt that gives users ideas of how they can continue to interact with Copilot. Suggestions are AI-generated and based in a user’s context to help teach Copilot’s capabilities in a conversational way.
whenToUse: Use suggestions to provide shortcuts for submitting prompts and to reply to or build on top of previous outputs. Suggestions are similar to prompt starters, but emphasize conversational context and multi-turn prompting instead of teaching prompt building.
behavior: Chat input autofill: Selecting a suggestion always inserts the prompt text into the chat input. Inserting into the chat input gives people the opportunity to edit the prompt either by changing it or expanding on it if needed.
Avoid buttons: Avoid using buttons within the output when a prompt would be submitted. Reserve buttons instead for system actions and confirmations.
Text wrapping: Suggestions will grow to fit their content. If content is longer than the width of the container, suggestion text will wrap.
Avoid text wrapping whenever possible to keep suggestions easy to scan.
Try to keep suggestion text to one line
Don’t include too much information because suggestions become hard to scan

Suggestion overflow: Multiple suggestions will expand to fill the width of their container. If there are more suggestions than will fit, limit them to two lines of suggestions in full chat experiences and three lines in sidecar experiences.
Limit suggestion overflow to two lines in full chat experiences
Limit suggestion overflow to three lines in sidecar experiences
Keep it short and actionable when possible: Keep text short to prevent text wrapping. Text should never truncate.
Progressive disclosure: Sometimes, a good prompt needs to be long and descriptive in order to get the best output. In these cases, don’t include the whole prompt in the suggestion.
Progressively disclosing the longer prompt helps people understand how to build robust prompts that can best accomplish a particular task.

do: Limit suggestion overflow to two lines in full chat experiences
Limit suggestion overflow to three lines in sidecar experiences
Keep it short and actionable when possible
Keep text short to prevent text wrapping.
dont: Avoid buttons: Avoid using buttons within the output when a prompt would be submitted. Reserve buttons instead for system actions and confirmations.
Avoid text wrapping whenever possible to keep suggestions easy to scan.
Don’t include too much information because suggestions become hard to scan

name: Chat output
description: Chat output shows the back and forth interactions between Copilot and the user. The Chat output pattern includes all subcomponents between the header and the chat input.
anatomy: Citations and references are dependent on the output that Copilot generates. They will only appear if Copilot references a graph entity.
behavior: Chat output is a highly composed Copilot pattern and, on its own, doesn’t dictate many UX behaviors. Instead, to understand how to help users get the most of this pattern, see the documentation for its component parts.

name: Citations and references
description: Citations and references help build trust for AI experiences by surfacing the information Copilot used to create its output. References represent the source grounding data. Citations connect a Copilot output to a reference.
whenToUse: Citations and references always appear in tandem.
states: Citations
Citations let a user know in context that Copilot has generated an answer from a graph entity. The citation connects the output to a reference listed in the output footer.
References
References represent source grounding data Copilot used to build a response.
behavior: Entity preview on hover: When hovering over a citation or a reference, users will see a popover showing a preview of that entity. Previews can either show summaries of the file, as seen below, or can have actionable suggestions within them to help users find an obvious next step.
App handoff on entity selection: When selecting a reference, that entity will open in its respective Office Web app, Teams, or Outlook.

Reference overflow: References are shown in the output footer until they reach the max width of their container. If there is overflow, use a Show more button to indicate that there are more references used to build the output that a user can interact with.
Naming references: References will match file names exactly. Exclude the document type from the reference name.
Reference icons: Use the icon slot to indicate what type of file the reference is.

do: Use the icon slot to indicate what type of file the reference is.

name: Copilot message
description: Copilot message is the Copilot response in conversational UX scenarios.
behavior: Latency and loading: To communicate that a message is still being generated, use the progress properties. This will trigger the loading state on the individual Copilot message.

Loading an immediate response: The Copilot title and AI disclaimer are hidden during the immediate response phase of the latency pattern. Copilot provides the user with a series of statements and the Copilot Loader until it’s ready to move into the streaming phase.
The submit button on the input turns into a stop button so that users might cancel the action Copilot is taking.

Streaming a response: When the streaming phase begins, the immediate response statements are replaced with the Copilot title and AI disclaimer. The Copilot Loader is appended to the bottom of the component and appears whenever Copilot needs a moment to continue processing the output.

Streaming below the fold: When the content generated by Copilot extends below the viewable area, a down button appears above of the output content. The Copilot Loader and the down button should not be visible at the same time.

Copilot messages output directly onto the main surface instead of in an elevated or contained card. In addition to the Copilot avatar, name, and AI disclaimer, placing the Copilot message on the main surface helps to create the distinction between a Copilot message and a message from another human.
Footnote: Copilot messages can contain footnotes that house contextual information or metadata related to that particular response. Footnotes are comprised of Sensitivity and Reference subcomponents.
Actions: Any actions related to that particular Copilot message appear at the bottom of the Copilot message, beneath the output text and footnote. Emphasize primary actions in this space.
accessibility: Focus: Pressing Enter on a focused Copilot message will trap and cycle focus within the message so that users can access the information and interactions within. Pressing Esc will move focus out of the Copilot message and back to the Copilot chat container so that users can move from message to message.
If there are available contextual actions on hover, they are also available on a focused message.

name: Sensitivity
description: Sensitivity indicates that a Copilot output is derived from sensitive data. Copilot generated responses will inherit the most restrictive sensitive from the sources it references.
states: Sensitivity icon
Place the sensitivity icon on a Copilot response or output to indicate that that output was generated from sensitive data. In chat, always include a citation linking to the source entity.
Sensitivity label
Use the sensitivity label on the relevant reference to indicate the sensitivity classification.
behavior: Sensitivity popover: On hover, the sensitivity popover shows the sensitivity label, which alerts users to the exact sensitivity level. The sensitivity popover also gives a brief summary of the file and its contents.

name: Timestamp
description: Timestamps divide messages by day in a chat thread.
behavior: Use relative timing until it exceeds one week. After that, use dates without the year until it exceeds one year.
For example:
Today, Yesterday, Wednesday, Tuesday, Monday
August 21, August 8, etc.
September 4, 2023

do: Use relative timing until it exceeds one week.

name: User message
description: The user message is the chat card that represents the user’s input to Copilot. User messages look identical to user messages in Teams to reinforce the mental model of synchronous conversation.
behavior: Secondary actions: User messages can have a secondary action menu available on focus or hover. This menu is not immediately discoverable and should be reserved for lesser actions like copying, bookmarking, or sharing.

Secondary actions are helpful when a user has a particular task they associate with that prompt, like saving it to reuse or sharing it with colleagues. Copilot actions should never appear in the hover menu.

name: Copilot FRE
description: The Copilot FRE is used to introduce Copilot the first time it becomes available to someone within a particular app or service. It is made up of the Fluent dialog combined with Fluent carousel, with some customizations.
whenToUse: If you want to introduce a new Copilot feature to someone who has already seen Copilot in your app or service, use prompt starters, zero-prompt, and/or the prompt guide instead.
behavior: Triggers: The Copilot FRE dialog is triggered when someone opens an app, file, or web service where Copilot is available to them for the first time.
If another FRE is being shown for the host app or service, postpone the Copilot FRE to the next session.
Dismissal: The FRE dialog is modal and blocking, that is, people must dismiss or complete the FRE before they can take any other action in the host app or service.
To dismiss it, they must select Close, Not now, or Try Copilot. Note that, in React, there is no X (Close) button, but in Win32, an X appears in the top right corner.
If they close the FRE by selecting Close or Not now, the FRE reappears the next time they open the app or service.
If they select Try Copilot, the FRE closes, the Copilot chat panel opens, and we don’t show the FRE again to that person.
To avoid annoying people, show the FRE a maximum of two times per platform, per app, and per user.

Placement: The Copilot FRE appears in the center of the app screen, in focus, with an overlay obscuring the app behind it. Because it is a modal dialog, users can’t interact with the content behind the FRE until it’s closed.
Anatomy: Each Copilot FRE page consists of:
Illustration that shows Copilot in context of the host app or service
Title, with a call to action for using Copilot
Body content, describing ways to use Copilot in the app
Temporary dismissal (Not now), or navigation (Previous) button
Progress indicator (page 1 of 2, page 2 of 2)
Navigation (Next) or completion (Try Copilot) button
The FRE introduces Copilot to new users with a summary of basic functionality, and tips on how to get started.
The FRE should consist of no more than two pages, because research has found that users rarely click through or pay attention to more than two pages in a FRE carousel.

Page 1 describes what you can do with Copilot: The content follows a template, with blank parts that can be modified per app to highlight the most common and useful scenarios for Copilot within that app.
Title: Starts with an action verb and describes the overall value for Copilot in that app.
Body:
accessibility: For screen readers, provide alt text and an ARIA description for the illustration on each page. Because learning new things requires cognitive energy, keep the information brief, conveying the general idea of the illustration, not every detail.
An ARIA description for the progress indicator states the page and total number of pages, for example, “Page 1 of 2”.
Do
For the illustration, provide ARIA text with a short, general description of what is being illustrated.
Don’t
Don’t go into unnecessary visual detail in ARIA descriptions for screen readers.

dont: Don’t go into unnecessary visual detail in ARIA descriptions for screen readers.

name: Entity cards
description: An entity is a content type that is stored in Substrate such as a file, meeting, or person. Entity cards contain AI generated insights and actions that represent the content in each entity and suggest next steps based on that content. Each type of entity card has variations that add new features.
whenToUse: Use entity cards to represent a document, meeting, or person stored in substrate. Don’t use entity cards to represent a prompt, action, or agent. If you need to represent a prompt, action, or agent, use the corresponding card type instead.
states: An entity card can present as a full horizontal or vertical card, an abbreviated vertical or horizontal card, a list item, a chicklet.
Document cards
Designed to represent people in an organization. May include details to summarize reasons for displaying each card.
People cards
Meeting cards
behavior: Relationship to Glance cards and AI Overviews: Entity cards, glance cards, and AI Overviews are all connected. One is an extension of the other and they work as building blocks to each other.
AI Insights: A team can choose to hide insights or quick actions by default. When insights are not visible at rest, selecting the AI sparkle button reveals them.
Quick actions: Users can access quick actions through the overflow menu. The buttons appear on hover, providing easy access to commonly used actions.

Handoff to app: Selecting either the title or product icon hands off users to the corresponding app. These interactions are commonly observed across Microsoft products but can be adapted to meet unique requirements.
Interactive preview: Selecting the “Play” button enables users to interact with the preview. For a PowerPoint file, this allows users to navigate through the slides in an expanded card view.

Width and height: Card width and height for web experiences should remain consistent. Card width should stay within 240 and 680 pixels while card height should stay within 580 pixels depending on the card type being used.

Content structure: Entity cards are meant to hold information about the entity in a way that prioritizes readability and consistency. Most elements are optional aside from the title, icon and backplate, and overflow menu to maintain the card’s function.
Required: Title + sensitivity label
Icon + backplate
Quick actions / Overflow
Optional: Metadata
Reason marker
Preview (static or interactive, play button appears on hover)
Insights or summary
Suggested actions
Additional Action
Reason marker: Reason markers are an optional element that let users know why they’re seeing a given Entity card.
Keep reason markers brief and to the point to avoid truncation and localization issues. Avoid repetition of any information already visible on the card.
AI Insights and summaries: AI Insights and summaries provide AI generated information about an entity. In full length cards, AI Insights are static.
Quick actions: Quick actions suggest next steps for the user based on the entity and the information provided in the insights.
accessibility: In insights-shy cards, the Insights button must be exposed in order to be accessible by the user. In general, revealing buttons only on hover is known to cause accessibility issues.

do: Use sentence-style capitalization—only capitalize the first word.

name: Ghost text
description: Ghost text, also known as placeholder text, helps provide guidance for user input. Once a user starts to type, the ghost text disappears.
whenToUse: Ghost text is intended to quickly and simply describe the action the user should take or help them understand the information Copilot needs to generate a good output.
behavior: Temporary and transient: Ghost text disappears once users begin to add their prompt. Because of this, it’s important to make sure that the information included is only helpful, not necessary for the user to complete the prompt.
Contextual changes: Ghost text may also change once the text area is selected, to give a new hint to the user and show them more ways to get value from Copilot.
In the zero state, the ghost text can encourage the user to start a draft.
Once Copilot has generated a draft, the ghost text can let the user know they can use Copilot to make changes.

Type ahead: There are times when Copilot will attempt to guess the remainder of a user’s prompt. These are prompt suggestions and aren’t ghost text, but behave in the same way by being transparent text and changing as a user types.

Use ghost text to give a short, supplementary hint for how to get the best response from Copilot or a clue as to how to move forward. Keep the content contextual to what the user is trying to accomplish.
Unlike prompt starters, ghost text doesn’t always have to be action oriented. Use your best judgement to discern what information would be most helpful to a user, a suggested action or a question.
Skip the period in placeholder text. For more info, see Periods in the Microsoft Writing Style Guide.
Ghost text can spark ideas by asking questions.
Ghost text can point to a path forward by suggesting actions.
accessibility: Don’t use ghost text for essential information that people will need in order to interact with Copilot. When someone focuses on the input, the placeholder disappears, and removing the prompt can make it difficult for some people, including those with cognitive impairments, to enter information.
Ghost text must be associated with an aria-label for assistive technologies.

dont: Don’t use ghost text for essential information that people will need in order to interact with Copilot. When someone focuses on the input, the placeholder disappears, and removing the prompt can make it difficult for some people, including those with cognitive impairments, to enter information.

name: Prompt starters
description: Prompt starters give people hints about how they can interact with Copilot. Use them to teach how to build prompts, give users a starting point for building a robust prompt, and show Copilot capabilities. Prompt starters are most often found in zero prompt experiences or inside the prompt library dialog.
whenToUse: Prompt starters teach people how to build effective prompts. If you need to help people build additional conversational context, use prompt suggestions.
states: Chat starter

The chat starter appears in side car experiences and sends the suggested prompt to the input where people can tweak it or send it to Copilot. They’re lightweight and straightforward and should help people accomplish and in-context task.
Library starter
The library starter is a more heavyweight card that provides more information and actions around a card. Use library starters to show people many different kinds of prompts they can try.
behavior: Textarea autofill: Selecting a prompt starter always inserts the prompt text into the textarea, even if no additional information is required to finish the prompt. If a reference is required, the CiQ menu will also open automatically.
Inserting into the textarea gives people the opportunity to edit the prompt either by changing it or expanding on it if needed.

Visual cues to fill in the blank: Prompt starters give users an idea of what a prompt can accomplish with data of their choice. To indicate that choice, there are different visual cues to direct people toward Microsoft Graph entities or free-form text entry.

Blue text or tags for Microsoft Graph entities: Entities that exist in the Microsoft Graph, like meetings, calendar events, emails, chats, and people, are represented by blue text. By default, the text is comms blue but can be changed to reflect the color of the product it appears in.

When a user selects a prompt starter that calls for a Microsoft Graph entry, the blue text doesn’t autofill into the textarea. Instead, the CiQ menu opens and has focus so that the user can choose the entity they want to complete the prompt.
Badge for CiQ
Blue text for CiQ

Gray texts in brackets for free-form entry: To prompt users to enter free-form text that doesn’t map to Microsoft Graph data points, use gray texts in brackets. The content of that text should be general so that the distinction between a free-form entry and graph data remains clear.

When a user selects a prompt starter that calls for free-form entry, the gray, bracketed text doesn’t autofill into the textarea. Instead, the cursor appears to suggest that the user can complete the prompt on their own.
Free-form entry in chat starters
Free-form entry in library starter
Chat starter limits: Don’t use more than three chat prompt starters. Space is limited so highlight the most helpful prompts.
Writing library starters: Prompt library starters tend to have more screen real estate that chat starters. Therefore, titles in library starters can be more descriptive.
Library starter body text summarizes a long, in-depth prompt that will appear in the input. Keep the starter body text brief, usually the first sentence of the larger prompt.
Writing chat starters: Prompts represent user agency. Use third person to represent a command to Copilot.
Include ellipses ( … ) to indicate that open-ended information should be added to complete the prompt. Try to truncate prompts at the end of a word and use a space before the ellipses.
If no additional information is required to submit the prompt, format content regularly.

dont: Don’t use more than three chat prompt starters. Space is limited so highlight the most helpful prompts.

name: System message
description: System messages are used in Copilot for messages from the system that need to sit outside the chat conversation. They are typically used to inform someone about an action related to the chat but occurring somewhere else or in the background.
whenToUse: If Copilot performs an action for the user that is visible in the main canvas without switching contexts, use chat output for this message instead. For system-level errors like Copilot being unavailable, use a message bar instead.
behavior: In handoff scenarios, the system message is triggered when the user chooses an action button in the Copilot chat that requires handoff, such as “Edit in Word” or “Create a policy.”
When handoff goes to a different app or service, a system message appears in both the initiating app chatS and the destination app chat, with slight variation in content to fit each context.

Placement and styling: After Copilot takes action on behalf of the user, the system message appears below the last message or option in the chat. It uses muted styling to deemphasize and differentiate it from the main conversation.
It may include an icon related to the action performed. For handoff messages, this is usually the Open icon, which indicates opening something in a different window or browser tab.
System messages are always written in third person, describing what Copilot did and where. The message is a full sentence, and ends with a period.
Handoff messages: System messages are most commonly used for handoffs, which can be used to:
Navigate to another page or file in the same app or service
Navigate to a different app or service (on the web, opens in a different tab)

When Copilot takes a requested action on behalf of the user and hands the user off to another page, file, app, or service to continue working, a system message appears in Copilot chat. This is called a handoff.
When the handoff goes to a different app or service in a new window or browser tab, separate messages, called bookends, appear in the originating and destination chat panes.

Handoff messages are tailored to fit the context where they appear. In the originating app, the message clarifies where the user will go to continue working, and in the destination app, they include where the action was initiated.
Each handoff message includes an action and a noun. The action is typically ”opened” or “created,” and the noun is the name of the page, guide, app, or location that Copilot opened.
The system message should also inform if any styling, content, filters, or fields were applied or altered by Copilot.
In bookended handoff messages, the action and noun text should be the same for both the initiating and receiving apps.
For the app initiating, describe where the noun will be handed off to.
For the receiving app, describe where the noun is coming from.

Shown in initiating app: In the initiating app, messages generally follow the format “Copilot/Copilot chat [verbed] an [object] in [destination app].” For messages about opening a different web page, use the phrase “…opened [destination] in a new browser tab.” Examples:
Copilot opened an email draft in Outlook. [origin: Word; destination: Outlook]
Copilot opened a workbook in Excel. [origin: Word; destination: Excel]
Copilot opened a presentation in PowerPoint. [origin: Copilot Chat; destination: PowerPoint]
accessibility: When the system message is in focus, pressing Enter moves focus to any focusable elements, such as a link, when present. Pressing Esc moves focus back to the whole system message.
By default, the system message announces “system message” followed by the contents of the message. An announcement property can optionally be added to announce a custom message.
